extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and authors of mathematical exposition (students, researchers, lecturers, and textbook authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing clear, honest, and well-organized mathematical exposition (papers, books, and lectures), covering diction, notation, theorem statements, proofs, and interactions with editors/audiences. Emphasizes readability, correct usage of technical language, and adaptation to medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty is the best policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mathematical language to make understanding easy; be honest about the status of statements and the difficulty of arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the purpose of style to 'smooth the reader's way' — clarity not pedantry. Do not gloss over difficulties: if a cumbersome computation is necessary, carry it out in public and sympathize with the reader (e.g., preface with 'unfortunately the only known proof is the following cumbersome computation'). When you state that something does not imply something else, do not leave the reader feeling cheated: indicate whether a counterexample will be supplied, give a reference if it's standard but irrelevant, or confess if you tried and failed to derive one. Use 'obvious' or 'easy to see' only when you truly think it is obvious: check later (after time has passed) or explain if it was accepted as obvious in seminar discussion; and above all, make sure the 'obvious' is true. Always tell the reader where each statement stands (proved, unproved, to be proved later, etc.). Emphasize important facts and minimize trivialities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Down with the irrelevant and the trivial
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid irrelevant assumptions, incorrect emphasis, and legalistic-but-insufficiently-explicit statements; treat trivial cases explicitly where needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not drag in irrelevant hypotheses (readers will ask what semisimplicity or unit has to do with an apparently obvious fact). Explicitly mention and if necessary exclude trivial cases (e.g., address 0 separately when it affects general behavior). State the theorem before proof: give introductory comments/definitions first, then the statement, then the proof. Keep theorem statements short and, whenever possible, to one sentence; avoid sprawling statements with many hypotheses and many conclusions — if hypotheses serve different conclusions, isolate and name the general concept. Avoid 'rambling' that hides where you are going and the 'hanging' theorem (announcing a theorem only after the proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: DO AND DO NOT REPEAT
rubrics_metrics.description: Use repetition deliberately: repeat wording to emphasize parallelism, but avoid needless verbal repetition and never repeat proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good repetition: reuse the same words in the same order across chapters when treating parallel theories to make differences stand out; if needed, rewrite earlier material for parallelism. Bad repetition: avoid saying the same thing slightly differently (it creates confusion about whether content is identical). Never repeat a proof — if proofs of different theorems share structure, extract and state a lemma that covers both and prove it once. Avoid shorthand 'see the proof of Theorem 1' without isolating the repeated idea as a lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: The editorial 'we' is not all bad
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer neutral declarative sentences, avoid 'one', use 'we' appropriately to mean author+reader, and avoid overuse of 'I'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best expository style is unobtrusive: use neutral constructions ('Since p, it follows that q') rather than 'one has'. The imperative can be effective ('To find q, multiply p by r.'), but use 'given' carefully (e.g., 'Given p, find g' not 'Given p, there is a g'). Let 'we' mean the author and reader (or lecturer and audience) — e.g., 'Using Lemma 2 we can generalize Theorem 1' is fine — but do not misuse 'we' for facts about the authors' research ('Our work on this result was done in 1969' is inappropriate unless multiple authors). Overuse of 'I' can seem arrogant; reserve it for short notes, historical remarks, or personal essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use words correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose logical and common words carefully since small words can alter mathematical meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous words: do not use 'any' in contexts where it is unclear whether existential or universal quantification is intended — replace with 'each' or 'every' or recast the sentence. Avoid lazy 'where' (it often signals an afterthought). Do not misuse 'equivalent' for informal relations between theorems (a theorem cannot be false; saying two theorems are 'equivalent' is logically imprecise). Avoid chained 'if ... then ... if ... then' constructions; recast as 'If p and q, then r' or other clearer forms. Think about the small words of common sense and use them precisely to avoid misleading readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical terms correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain and respect precise technical meanings (functions vs values, sequence vs countable set, contain vs include); be consistent and avoid inventing unnecessary new terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example distinctions: treat a function and its values as different things ('the function z ↦ z^2 + 1 is even' rather than 'the function z^2 + 1 is even'). Use 'sequence' only when the ordered-nature matters; otherwise say 'countable set' or 'countably infinite set'. Consider reserving 'contain' for '⊃' and 'include' for '⊂' if you adopt a terminology — consistency comforts readers. Recommendations: (1) avoid creating new technical terms when possible; (2) think carefully about any new terms and consult references; (3) use old terms correctly and consistently while minimizing obtrusive pedantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize notation: prefer prose where possible, avoid irrelevant symbols, and do not leave free variables dangling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best notation is 'no notation' — pretend you are speaking and use symbols only when necessary. Avoid irrelevant symbols in statements (e.g., do not introduce a letter just for the statement when it contributes nothing). Do not leave free variables in displayed sentences; bind them or omit the symbol. Be stingy with labels for displays: label only when you'll refer back; irrelevant labels waste the reader's attention. In induction and matrix arguments, prefer indicating the typical step (e.g., prove 3×3 case) and 'and so on' rather than filling pages with repetitious arrays of dots. Prefer forward proofs (start from hypotheses and proceed forward) rather than backward proofs that are machine-verifiable but hard for humans to follow. When repeated techniques appear across proofs, find a lemma instead of copying computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbols correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent in how symbols are read and translated into words, punctuate symbolic sentences like verbal ones, and attend to layout and page appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a symbol consistently so its verbal translation is the same (e.g., read '∈' as 'is in'). Don't mix readings in the same sentence. Punctuate equations and symbolic clauses as you would verbal clauses — separate them from neighbors and avoid overworking a comma or period that causes backtracking. Never start a sentence with a bare symbol; if necessary put the denoted word in apposition ('The set X belongs to the class C, ...'). Use 'then' with 'if' in mathematical contexts to aid comprehension. Attend to page layout: balance prose and displays so the page neither looks like solid prose nor computational hash; intersperse enough displays to give the eye a rest but keep ample prose so the reader isn't drowned in symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: All communication is exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat books, articles, lectures, and letters as forms of exposition with the same basic problems: content, aim, organization, and the details of grammar, diction, and notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt exposition to medium: a lecture differs from a printed paper by the hearer's shorter attention span, inability to re-read, and the blackboard's visual growth; avoid long computations in lectures and plan blackboard use so material 'grows' naturally (don't cram the board before speaking). For printed work, people can re-read and check proofs; for lectures, omit or summarize computations and emphasize clarity and narrative. The same organization and stylistic rules apply across media, but apply them with attention to audience and medium constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend your style
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must be prepared to stand up to editorial assistants and copyreaders who apply mechanical rules that can change meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An editor can be invaluable, but editorial assistants may mechanically apply typographical or stylistic rules that introduce errors (e.g., changing 'measure-preserving' by removing a hyphen, or reversing a word order and changing meaning). Be prepared to 'defend your style' — explain usage choices (hyphens, punctuation relative to quotes, ordering that affects logic). Mechanical style rules (typographical decrees) can be harmful; authors should go forearmed into negotiations with copyeditors and be ready to correct changes that alter logical or mathematical meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stop (finish the work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the difficulty of stopping and finishing a book or manuscript; the final step is to stop writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's last task is to finish the writing — knowing when to stop is hard but essential. This admonition is a practical reminder that part of good exposition is completing and finalizing the work rather than endlessly revising.
